summary.text: Snow is solid precipitation made of ice crystals that grow while suspended in the air, usually in clouds, then fall and pile up on the ground.
Crystals form when tiny supercooled cloud droplets freeze, and flakes grow differently with the temperature and humidity they fall through, so they differ from one another.
Snow affects daily life and nature, from keeping roads and wings clear to feeding rivers when it melts and insulating plants and animals in winter.

items.prompt: Tiny cloud droplets can stay liquid far below the usual freezing point. What holds them back from freezing?

options.label: Dissolved salt lowers their freezing point
The thin air in clouds stops ice forming
A few molecules must first line up like ice
Their constant falling keeps them too warm

items.explain: To freeze, a few molecules in a droplet must come together by chance in an ice-like arrangement, which then acts as a nucleus.

items.prompt: In early winter, cold air blows across a wide lake whose water is still warmer than the air. Where does the heaviest snow fall?

options.label: On the upwind shore
On the downwind shore
Over the middle of the lake
Evenly all around the lake

items.explain: The air picks up water vapor from the warmer lake, rises, freezes and drops snow on the downwind shores.

items.prompt: Moist wind is forced up one side of a mountain range. How does the far, sheltered side compare for snow?

options.label: It gets more snow from colder air
It gets the same snow as the windward side
It gets snow only on clear nights
It gets less, as the air is drier and warmer

items.explain: Rising air cools and drops its moisture on the windward side, leaving drier, warmer air on the leeward side.

items.prompt: Snowflakes follow similar patterns, yet they differ from one another. Why?

options.label: Each meets changing temperature and humidity as it falls
Each forms from a different kind of water
Each is shaped by the wind once it lands
Each breaks apart in its own way on the ground

items.explain: Water molecules join a flake at different rates and in different patterns depending on the temperature and humidity along its fall.

items.prompt: A large low-pressure system crosses a Northern Hemisphere continent in winter. Which side of it usually gets the most snow?

options.label: The southern side
The eastern side
The northern side
The western side

items.explain: In the Northern Hemisphere, the northern side of a low-pressure area produces the most snow.

items.prompt: After a heavy snowfall, mice and small plants under the snowpack make it through a bitter cold spell. How does the snow help?

options.label: It gives off heat as it slowly melts
It feeds them water all winter
It blocks out all the sunlight
It forms an insulating layer over them

items.explain: Snow provides an insulating layer in winter under which plants and animals survive the cold.
